title: How do pharmaceutical companies make money, and what matters in a pharma case?
description: Pharma economics for case interviews: R&D pipelines, patents and generics, payers and reimbursement, launch uptake, with a worked patent-cliff example.
hook: Pharmaceutical companies make money by spending years and billions of dollars developing drugs, most of which fail, then earning high margins on the few that succeed while patents keep cheaper copies off the market. A pharma case usually turns on three things: the strength of the pipeline, what happens when a big drug loses its patent, and the gap between a drug being approved and patients actually getting it, which depends on doctors and on whoever pays.
body:
How pharma makes money

Developing a new medicine typically takes 10 to 15 years, and only about 1 in 10 candidates that enter clinical trials reaches the market. The industry body IFPMA puts the average cost at about $2.6B per approved medicine once the cost of failures is included (IFPMA facts and figures). A successful drug then earns very high gross margins, because making each pill is cheap compared with the research behind it.

That high margin lasts only while the drug is protected. Patents run for 20 years from filing, but companies file early, before trials, so the period of exclusive sales after launch is much shorter. When protection ends, generic copies (or biosimilars, for biological drugs) arrive. The US FDA found that generic prices fall about 39% below the brand's price with one generic competitor, about 79% with four, and more than 95% with six or more (FDA analysis). That collapse is the patent cliff.

Who decides

  • Doctors prescribe, and change habits slowly.
  • Patients take the drug, and may stop early (adherence).
  • Payers (governments, national health systems, insurers) decide whether to pay for it, at what net price, and for which patients.

The person choosing, the person using and the person paying are three different people. Many launch problems are really payer problems, not marketing problems.

A worked example: the patent cliff

An illustrative company has a drug selling $2B a year, 30% of its revenue, so total revenue is about $6.7B. Generics launch and the drug's sales fall 80% within two years, to $400M. The company loses $1.6B, about 24% of total sales, unless new drugs fill the gap. This is why pipeline strength drives pharma strategy, and why big companies buy biotechs with promising late-stage drugs.

A worked example: from approval to patients

A new drug treats a disease affecting 200,000 people in a market. Work down the funnel, using illustrative assumptions:

  • 60% are diagnosed: 120,000.
  • 50% of those meet the drug's eligibility criteria: 60,000.
  • 40% of those have reimbursed access: 24,000.
  • 25% of those are prescribed it: 6,000 patients.

At $12,000 net revenue per patient per year, that is $72M a year, if everyone stays on treatment all year. If the average patient stays nine months, it is $54M. Multiplying 200,000 patients by the list price would overstate the opportunity many times over, and would ignore the confidential rebates that make net price lower than list price.

Typical pharma case questions

  • Why is a new drug selling below forecast? (walk the funnel and find the biggest gap against plan)
  • Should we acquire a biotech with a promising drug? (see M&A cases)
  • How should we prepare for a patent expiry?
  • How should we price a new treatment? (value to patients and payers, competitor prices)

What a strong answer sounds like

Weak: "Sales are below forecast, so we should increase marketing to doctors."
Strong: "I'd compare each stage of the patient funnel with the plan: diagnosed, eligible, reimbursed, prescribed and still on treatment. If the gap is in reimbursement, more marketing to doctors won't help; we need better evidence for payers."

Common mistakes

  • Treating approval as access. Regulatory approval says the drug may be sold. It does not mean payers will fund it or doctors will prescribe it.
  • Using list price. Net price after rebates and discounts is what the company earns.
  • Ignoring failure risk. A drug in trials is worth its value if approved multiplied by the chance of approval, minus the costs still to spend.
  • Seeing only price in a patent expiry. Generics cut both the brand's volume share and its net price. Responses include new uses for the drug, new formulations, cost cuts or buying pipeline, and each needs its own business case.

Practise

1. A company with $5B of revenue has a $1.5B drug losing patent protection. Sales of the drug are expected to fall 70% within two years. What share of company revenue is at risk?

Show the answer

Lost sales: $1.5B × 70% = $1.05B. Share of revenue: $1.05B ÷ $5B = 21%. The question that follows is what in the pipeline can replace it, and when.

2. In the funnel above, the launch plan assumed 60% of eligible patients would have reimbursed access. Actual access is 40%. How much of the revenue gap does that explain?

Show the answer

Planned patients: 60,000 × 60% × 25% = 9,000. Actual: 6,000. The gap of 3,000 patients × $12,000 = $36M a year comes entirely from access. The fix is payer evidence and pricing, not sales reps.

3. A biotech's only asset is a drug in late-stage trials. If approved, its future profits are worth $500M today. It needs $200M more of trial costs before the result is known, and has a 60% chance of approval. The seller wants $250M. Is that a good price?

Show the answer

Expected value: 60% × $500M − $200M = $100M. At $250M the buyer would overpay by about $150M unless it has other reasons, such as cost savings, a stronger sales force for the drug, or other assets in the deal.

Where to practise next

For the hospital side of healthcare, read hospital and health system cases. The acquisition framework and pricing framework cover the two most common pharma case types, and the Corvane Medical case applies deal logic to a medical devices merger.
